speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, November 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-168, to amend the Criminal Code -Mr. Pennell-Mr. Rinfret in the chair.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext: Order. House again in committee of the whole on Bill No. C-168, to amend the Criminal Code. When the house rose on Thursday, November 23, clause 2 of the bill was under consideration. Shall clause 2 carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Carried.
On clause 2-Approval by governor in council of release after commutation of sentence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was asking some questions of the Solicitor General on November 23 when ten o'clock arrived and we were discussing clause 2 of this bill. I stated, as hon. members will find in Hansard, that I still had some questions I wished to ask on clause 2. Clause 2 reads as follows:
Subsection (3) of section 656 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
" (3) Notwithstanding any other law or authority, a person in respect of whom a sentence of death has been commuted to imprisonment for life or a term of imprisonment or a person upon whom a sentence of imprisonment for life has been imposed as a minimum punishment, shall not be released during his life or such term, as the case may be, without the prior approval of the governor in council."
My first question to the Solicitor General is this. The clause reads, "a person in respect of whom a sentence of death has been commuted to ... a term of imprisonment," and so on, evidently meaning less than life imprisonment. How many commutations have there been to less than life imprisonment in the case of convicted murderers sentenced to be hanged?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext: To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Chairman, there have been no cases in which the person convicted of murder has had his sentence commuted to less than life imprisonment. However, my officials will be with me in a few moments and I hope then to be in a position to confirm this answer.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
I am interested in this question for the simple reason that when the Queen commuted the execution order against Lepine in Manitoba in the 1870's it was commuted to a term of two years plus the loss of
November 29, 1967

civil rights. Inasmuch as we have been advised that the cabinet itself pass on all paroles for people who have had their sentences commuted to life imprisonment after ten years in prison, I was wondering whether there were any convicted murderers who had been given commuted sentences of less than ten years. The problem then arises, when would they be referred to the cabinet for decision on whether parole should be granted. We have the Lepine case as a precedent. I ask that question in all sincerity.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am advised by the officials that within the memory of persons working in the department now there has never been a case where a sentence of death has been commuted to less than life imprisonment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext: I am quite interested in this question, in view of the fact that the cabinet has been paroling convicted murderers after they have served a life sentence of eight years, ten months and one day, based on the figures produced in the House of Commons by the Solicitor General himself. Why do they have these words in the proposed bill, "or a term of imprisonment," not specifically life imprisonment? Are they now going to impose terms of imprisonment of less than ten years which would equal the eight years, ten months and one day of life sentences in the past 13 cases? Why is that phrase "or a term of imprisonment" put in this bill if there is no recollection of a convicted murderer having had his sentence commuted to less than a term of life imprisonment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
The proposed clause 2 is drafted to meet the conditions set out in section 656 of the Criminal Code wherein it states:
The governor in council may commute a sentence of death to imprisonment in the penitentiary for life, or for any term of years not less than two years, or to imprisonment in a prison other than a penitentiary for a period of less than two years.
I also wish to make it clear that I am not disputing the hon. member's statement that there have been cases where by commutation the sentence has been reduced to less than life. All I am saying is that my officials are not aware of any such case since they have been serving with the government.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am indebted to the Solicitor General for having read the section of the law. It points out that the governor in council may commute a sentence 27053-306
Amendment Respecting Death Sentence to a period of not less than two years in penitentiary, which includes anything from a little more than two years upwards to ten years. The other day the Solicitor General advised us that an order in council had been passed to the effect that the cabinet could not consider paroling a convicted man under sentence of life imprisonment until he had served at least ten years of his life sentence. If a man sentenced to life imprisonment must serve ten years of his life sentence, is there no possibility of parole before the expiration of his term for the man who has been committed to a term of not less than two years nor more than ten, which is much less than life imprisonment? When does the cabinet consider the question of parole for him? If his commuted sentence is say eight years, does he serve the full eight years because the cabinet, we are told, is not to consider this matter until he has served ten years?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would think it would be highly unlikely that the governor in council, having passed an order in council setting a minimum of ten years as the period to be served before a person becomes eligible for parole after receiving a capital sentence, would commute to less than ten years. It is not likely they would go contrary to the order in council passed in 1964.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
I may say I have seen the cabinet reverse itself in this very house in less than four hours. My only reply to the Solicitor General's statement is that it confirms his statement that this is a poorly drawn bill.
I should like to ask another question in connection with clause 2. We are told he shall not be released during his life or such term, as the case may be, without the prior approval of the governor in council. In answer to a question the other day the Solicitor General said such a case could not be referred to the governor in council until the ten years had been served. We who live in the province of Ontario and have children are very well aware of the fact a driver's licence can be issued to a young person at the age of 16. However, we have a regulation in the province of Ontario to the effect that when a child turns 15 years and 6 months he may be given a learner's permit. The idea is that during the six months between 15 years and 6 months and 16 years of age the child will be able to learn to drive a car on the public highways so that when he turns 16 years of age he will be able to get a driver's
4848	COMMONS
Amendment Respecting Death Sentence licence. Everyone knows what a world that opens up to the young.
I should like to ask the Solicitor General this question. In view of the fact that anyone who is serving life imprisonment for murder may not be paroled until he has served ten years, will the cabinet demand that he serve ten years in full before the parole board considers hope of parole and then refer the matter to the cabinet for final decision or will the parole board be given instructions that after eight years, ten months and one day they had better start considering parole for this man who has been sentenced to life imprisonment? If they decide that he should be given parole, can he be sprung by the cabinet at the end of the tenth year of his sentence, rather than have the poor fellow languish in jail after having completed ten years and then have the parole board consider the matter and then refer it to the cabinet? Under circumstances such as those, the poor devil might be in prison as long as 12 years because it may take the parole board and the cabinet two years to come to a decision to spring him. Will there be a provision such as exists in Ontario for young drivers which will enable the matter to be settled before the ten years are up so that the man can be sprung by the cabinet at the end of the tenth year or will he have to serve his full ten years before the matter of parole can be considered?
The other day I mentioned to the minister of immigration that we have a highly moral society. We keep European thieves out of this country so they will not be a blemish on our moral picture, but we parole convicted Canadian murderers amongst the people so that we can not only rehabilitate them but perhaps they will rehabilitate us. The question is, when will the parole board start considering the question of parole for this man, before the ten years are up so he will not have to serve one extra day beyond ten years, or will the board start considering the matter at the end of ten years imprisonment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the National Parole Board is an autonomous body. This government, and I am satisfied all other governments, have scrupulously respected the integrity of the board. No matter of parole is brought to the attention of the governor in council until the parole board takes the initiative. If the parole board reaches the conclusion that the case is not one for parole, the governor in council hears nothing of it. If they feel favourably inclined toward the

DEBATES	November 29, 1967
case, then it is forwarded to the office of the Solictior General who in turn brings it before his colleagues in cabinet.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have just one more question on clause 2. We are told this person shall not be released during his life or such term, as the case may be, without the prior approval of the governor in council. Is this a threat or a promise? Is it a promise that he will be sprung at the end of ten years or is it a threat that the cabinet, in all seriousness, in the certain way in which they consider every problem of the day, will dwell on the problem of parole for months and months so that he will have to fear inactivity on the part of the cabinet in connection with something which he hopes from this cabinet which has let people out after eight years, ten months and one day? Again I ask, does that phrase, "without prior approval of the governor in council", hold out a hope, a promise or a threat for the prisoner?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps it would be helpful if I pointed out that in non-capital cases the question of parole is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the National Parole Board and does not come to the governor in council. It is only in capital cases where the sentence has been commuted that the matter is referred to the cabinet. This new clause will make it necessary for all cases, both capital and non-capital, to be referred, and parole shall not be granted unless there is approval by the governor in council in addition to the approval of the National Parole Board.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just want to express a thought or two about the intention of the clause before us. I say at once that I do not know what the percentage figure is in connection with rehabilitation. In other words, I cannot say how many individuals who, having been convicted of a crime and sentenced, have successfully undergone rehabilitation. We talk in terms of 70 per cent or 80 per cent being recidivists, so presumably 20 per cent or 30 per cent represents the degree of success. These figures include criminals generally and not particularly those people who may have committed capital or non-capital murder.
I am quite sure that if during the time our penal system has been in existence we had followed the philosophy advocated by the hon. member for York-Humber we would undoubtedly be in a deficit position with respect to rehabilitation. I do not care to

Mr. Chairman, I should like the Solicitor General to tell the committee why paragraph (a) of clause 3, subclause 1, was included in the bill. If I understand paragraph (a) correctly, it seems that cases of alleged murder already before the courts or cases in which proceedings have been commenced before, this act comes into force are to be proceeded with as if the law is that which existed before this bill passed. This would mean that if in cases already commenced but which will not actually come to trial for a few months the accused is found guilty of capital murder, the judge is called upon to sentence the accused to death.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It strikes me as rather strange that we would call upon our courts to pass such sentences, parliament having made the decision that it does not favour the application of capital punishment except in two restricted cases. I find it hard to believe that the cabinet would countenance a death sentence when parliament has decided against capital punishment. Where a death sentence has been passed I should think that commutation would be almost automatic. It it not a farce, then, to ask judges, juries and courts to handle capital cases in the next few months as though the law had not been changed? Since parliament has made its decision about capital punishment and since in all likelihood the cabinet will commute any death sentence, will it not be a bit of a farce for a judge to put on his black gloves and so on and sentence a man to death at any time during the next two or three months?
I think that the Solicitor General and I are on the same wavelength about what ought to be done. I want to know why this provision is to continue in force. It seems to me that clause 3(3)(a) ought to be eliminated and clause 3 ought to be redrafted. I am not proposing an amendment. I am merely saying that this provision ought not to be in this bill.
(Mr. Howard.]

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while the
Solicitor General is thinking of the answer to my hon. friend's question it might be appropriate for me to add a word to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said.
It seems to me, in the situation he has drawn to our attention, that our judges, juries and courts will be placed in a false position so far as the law is concerned. The hon. member for Bow River in general terms, when speaking on an earlier amendment, spoke about the mockery of the administration of justice. Parliament has changed the law. For parliament, through the provisions of clause 3(l)(a), to call on a judge to pronounce a solemn sentence of death, in the light of the change in the law, is to make a mockery of the administration of justice and to bring it into disrepute. The death penalty is not the appropriate penalty in such circumstances.
With the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I urge the Solicitor General to reconsider this matter. What is the administrative difficulty of making the new law applicable at a certain date? The new legislation ought to apply to all capital murder trials that take place after that date. We ought not to tolerate the present situation where charges may have been laid and where the accused may be tried with the old law still being applicable.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would also like to say a few words about subclause (3). I should appreciate it if the minister would indicate to the house and to all Canadians the meaning of commutation of the death penalty.
The legislation provides in general that, in the case of an individual sentenced to life imprisonment, the governor in council may reduce the term of imprisonment, further to a report to this effect from the National Parole Board.
The public-as I came to realize during the week-ends I spent in my riding-was asking this very question. They wanted to know, in the case of an individual sentenced to life imprisonment, what standards and criteria the minister will use to commute his sentence.
Will the minister have to rely solely on the reports of the parole board or will he try to set up another organization which would review the recommendations submitted by the board to the cabinet?
I know that the parole board performs a tremendous task. Its members are only
November 29, 1567	COMMONS
human and make mistakes sometimes, but I feel, when the life sentence of a dangerous criminal is to be reduced by ten or fifteen years, that the minister should take every precaution to ensure that its decision is not detrimental to society in general.
I should like to know whether the minister will maintain the National Parole Board as it now stands and whether he will accept the recommendations of the board on the commutation of the sentence of someone who is sentenced to life imprisonment.
I should also like to know whether the minister intends to alter the organization of the National Parole Board or if he will set up another body to reassure the public that the recommendations of the board have been seriously considered in depth, because I know the minister cannot go into all the details when he is asked for parole. He must rely on the parole board and it is impossible, even inhuman, to ask the minister to consider all the details in order to make an objective recommendation to the cabinet.
I should also like to know whether the minister intends to check in detail and in depth the recommendations of the National parole board and what criteria he will use as a basis for his recommendations to the cabinet for a commutation of sentence for someone sentenced to life imprisonment.

We hope that by taking action under clause 5 when this bill becomes law it

In recent times the government has announced increases in the mortgage rates under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. All these things have caused us to wonder whether the members of the government are really sincere in their statements


that they want to encourage home ownership. As the situation now stands, those in the low income brackets, or even in the medium income brackets, find it almost impossible to proceed with their building plans and to build their own homes. I do not believe we are giving them very much encouragement because it seems that every measure introduced and every announcement made in this regard make it more difficult for them to proceed with such plans.
As I have said, we support the proposal that the government should give immediate consideration to the feasibility of allowing residential taxes to be deductible from federal personal income tax. We also support the idea that mortgage interest should also be included as an exemption. Under our present system a person pays in capital and interest an amount double the initial cost. Therefore, in considering this entire program and the desirability of home ownership, because of its social as well as its economic ramifications, I believe mortgage interest should be included as well even though the hon. member did not see fit to include it in his motion.
I should like to join with the hon. member for Parkdale in his impassioned plea that members of all parties support this resolution. I know he is sincere in presenting it and in making this plea to hon. members. I trust that no member on the government side will stand up and talk out the motion. I hope it will be permitted to come to a vote. Last night a measure was defeated which would have added to the burden of the taxpayers by increasing postage rates. This motion, if adopted, will help to decrease that burden. I hope that in this instance the member on the government side who has introduced this motion will have the support of the house and that it will be passed before six o'clock.

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF RESIDENTIAL. TAXES
speechtext:
Proposed Deduction from Income Tax which accrues to an individual through his own use or consumption of an income generating asset. As I said, no matter how interesting such a concept might be in a theoretical sense, certainly if you are not getting income which you can spend or use to improve your living standard you are not getting any benefit from it. The Carter commission will have to go a long way to persuade most of the reasonable people in this country that they are getting a benefit from some type of imputed income in respect of which they are spared the opportunity of paying income tax, particularly having regard to a home which they own themselves and in which they live.
The Carter commission overlooked the basic point that the great majority of home owners do not purchase their homes for investment purposes but for the purpose of shelter. If a home or dwelling were purchased as an investment then one could possibly see its argument, but the fact of the matter is that obviously the overwhelming majority of people who own their own homes bought them to provide themselves with shelter. Their aim was to get an adequate roof over their heads. I do not think it is sensible at all to treat a home owned and occupied by an individual as a form of investment.
Another argument is made, and again I am not stating it as my argument, that if a person vacated his house he could rent it and get income from it on which he would have to pay taxes. Of course, if a person vacated his house he would have to go out and rent or buy another one and he would have to get the money to pay the rent or to purchase another house. In any event, as a practical matter a person occupying his own home would in very few cases have the means to permit him to go out and rent another home or buy another home while putting his original dwelling up for rent or sale as a commercial matter. This is simply not a realistic possibility at all.
As the hon. member for Parkdale put it so well, and other members also, I think home ownership is something that should be encouraged. A person who owns his own home obviously has an interest in and a concern for it which does not exist in the same way on the part of an individual renting an apartment or a dwelling of another sort. The decision to rent or buy is a personal and optional one, and it therefore cannot be said that people who decide to rent, having made a personal decision after taking into

consideration the possibility that if the law is changed they cannot deduct their property taxes, are being treated in an unfair way or would be treated in an unfair way if they were not able to make a similar type of deduction. But in any event the hon. member for Parkdale has pointed out that his resolution implies the working out of a scheme that would afford similar benefits to someone renting an apartment or a house. Of course, we should remember that many people who own their own homes are people with limited incomes-people on fixed incomes and people who are retired. For these people the burden of residential taxes is very real. It falls on them much more heavily proportionately than on people who have other income besides their pensions and whose income may not change for years at a time. This certainly should be kept in mind.
So the argument of the Carter commission that the person who owns and occupies his own dwelling is getting some benefit because he does not have to pay income tax on an imputed income is one which the majority of the people of this country will find very hard to accept. Most people will take the common sense view that if they are not getting the income and are not deliberately forgoing it, it is certainly not a benefit. The fact that they are not being asked to pay income tax on income they do not get is nothing for which the royal commission or the government can take credit. This is an interesting argument in the form of a sort of verbal sleight of hand but, as I said, it is one which I think the population of this country will find very hard to accept.
Another argument that may very well be raised against the proposal of the hon. member for Parkdale is that those people who are more affluent and have larger incomes and larger homes will get a greater benefit because if a person has a larger home, one with 20 rooms or more, he will pay larger property taxes and thus get a greater benefit than someone who has a more modest cottage elsewhere. In my opinion there is a ver>
simple answer to this argument, namely, to place a maximum on the amount of property tax that can be deducted for income tax purposes.

speechtext:
Thank you. This proves my point, Mr. Speaker, that this type of discussion here is very constructive and will put suggestions before those charged with the responsibility of formulating tax policy in a way that otherwise could not be done. We already have something like this in our income tax law. If I am not mistaken there is an upper limit on the amount that can be deducted with respect to donations for charitable purposes. I think there is also an upper limit on the amount that can be deducted with respect to money paid out for medical expenses. Actually it is a percentage. But the point I am trying to make is that this principle exists already in our income tax law.
When we proceed to consider changes of the type contemplated by the hon. member for Parkdale the argument that will be raised against them by some-and it is not one being made by me-is that the more affluent and wealthy people will receive a proportionately greater benefit. This argument can be dealt with by placing a ceiling or upper limit on the amount of property tax that would be subject to deduction.
There is one argument that may be raised which may be somewhat more difficult to answer. There are those who may come forward and say that by accepting the suggestion of the hon. member for Parkdale a certain amount of tax revenue which we now receive will be lost. Of course, to carry out the programs of the government which the public desire, tax revenue is necessary. I think the answer to that argument is to review our tax system to see whether there are areas which are not bearing their fair share of taxes, and try to make up the difference from these sources. Obviously it would not be sufficient merely to bring in the change proposed by the hon. member for Parkdale. At the same time we do this we would have to take a look at our tax system generally and make sure that the revenue which would not be obtained as a result of the change which I think the hon. member is constructively proposing would be made up through some other source.

I think this is why the approach of the government in planning to present to us a white paper setting forth its views on the proposals of the Carter commission is very constructive. Rather than dealing with these things in a piecemeal manner-I make this comment not in a critical fashion at all with respect to the constructive suggestion of the hon. member for Parkdale-we will have a package brought before us and will be able to see the effect of any change on other areas of our tax policy.
I believe this is a very good way to go about it, especially since it is my understanding that the government's white paper will be referred to a committee of this house for study. In the course of that study we will hold public hearings and be able to hear not only from members of this house but also from people from the general public sector. Speaking personally, I hope this may be a precedent for an evolution in tax policy.
The United States goes about making budgets in a much more open fashion than we do. I am not saying I am completely familiar with their method. However, 1 think they bring down a budget document, or rather the president presents a budget message to congress and congress holds a lengthy series of public hearings. There is quite a public discussion before the laws are passed, and often many amendments are made. I do not think this method shakes to its roots the financial structure of that country.
It is my feeling, now that I have been here for several years, that whatever may be said for our present system of budget-making there is a lot to be said for moving forward and having a more open system than we have at the present time when making and changing tax laws. I hope the remarks already made in the house by the Minister of Finance with regard to handling the recommendations of the Carter commission may be an omen of further development in our parliamentary system with respect to budget-making.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I again want to commend the hon. member for Parkdale for his very constructive proposal. I think a proposal of this type would do a lot to remove the burden which I believe already falls too heavily on people who occupy their own homes, many of whom are on very limited incomes. Certainly there are needs for education, the building of roads and social welfare at the municipal level. These matters are very important. But 1 think the
